[THOUGHT] I need the chief complaint and duration to orient the differential. This single question will guide further focused questions and tests efficiently.

[QUERY] What is your main problem/complaint and how long have you had it?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient presents with a complaint of severe vulvar itching that has been gradually worsening over the course of the past year.

[RESPONSE] My main problem is severe vulvar itching, and it has been gradually worsening over the past year.

[THOUGHT] Age and menopausal status are critical for narrowing causes (e.g., lichen sclerosus common in postmenopausal; atrophic vaginitis in older women). I'll first obtain the patient's age.

[QUERY] How old are you?

[THOUGHT] In a 60-year-old with chronic progressive vulvar pruritus, the single most critical next step is a targeted vulvar physical examination to differentiate causes (lichen sclerosus or planus, contact dermatitis, eczematous disease, candidiasis less likely chronic, or vulvar neoplasia). Visual inspection and palpation will identify white atrophic plaques, scarring or fusion, erosions, hyperkeratosis, excoriations, erythema, or any suspicious ulcerated/nodular lesions that guide diagnosis and need for biopsy.

[TEST] Perform a detailed vulvar examination (visual inspection and gentle palpation) and report specific findings: presence/location of white patches/plaques, thinning/atrophy, erythema, erosions/ulcerations, scarring or labial fusion, hyperkeratotic nodules, excoriations, and whether the perianal area is involved; also include brief speculum exam notes about vaginal mucosa.

Thinning/atrophy:

Erythema:
Normal

Erosions/ulcerations:
Normal

Scarring or labial fusion:

Hyperkeratotic nodules:
Normal

Excoriations:
Normal

Palpation findings:
12. The lesions are palpable.
13. The vulvar area is tender to touch.

Speculum exam — vaginal mucosa:
Normal

[THOUGHT] A 60-year-old with progressive, severe vulvar itching for a year who has thin, dry white plaque-like lesions on the vulva, atrophy of the labia minora, clitoral retraction, and pale, wrinkled perianal involvement is most consistent with vulvar lichen sclerosus. The classic "parchment-like" white plaques, labial atrophy/fusion, and figure-of-eight vulvar–perianal distribution strongly favor lichen sclerosus over lichen planus (which more often has erosions and vaginal involvement) or chronic dermatitis. Vaginal mucosa is normal, which also supports lichen sclerosus. Given the chronicity and scarring changes, this is the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Vulvar lichen sclerosus
